etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English taske (“task, tax”), from Old Northern French tasque, (compare Old French variant tasche), from Medieval Latin tasca, alteration of taxa, from Latin taxāre (“censure; charge”). Doublet of tax.

definitions.definition: A piece of work done as part of one’s duties.

quote.citation: 2013 July 19, Ian Sample, “Irregular bedtimes may affect children's brains”, in The Guardian Weekly, volume 189, number 6, page 34:
quote.text: Irregular bedtimes may disrupt healthy brain development in young children, according to a study of intelligence and sleeping habits.  ¶ Going to bed at a different time each night affected girls more than boys, but both fared worse on mental tasks than children who had a set bedtime, researchers found.

definitions.definition: A single action undertaken by a given agent.

quote.citation: 2002 April 30, “Zeno’s Paradoxes”, in Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy:
quote.text: [T]here is a well-defined run in which the stages of Atalanta’s run are punctuated by finite rests, arguably showing the possibility of completing an infinite series of finite tasks in a finite time

quote.citation: 2013 August 10, “A new prescription”, in The Economist, volume 408, number 8848:
quote.text: As the world's drug habit shows, governments are failing in their quest to monitor every London window-box and Andean hillside for banned plants. But even that Sisyphean task looks easy next to the fight against synthetic drugs. No sooner has a drug been blacklisted than chemists adjust their recipe and start churning out a subtly different one.

definitions.definition: (computing) A process or execution of a program.

quote.citation: 1593, anonymous author, The Life and Death of Iacke Straw […], Act I:
quote.text: Art thou the Collector of the Kings taske?  […]  Thou haſt thy taske money for all that be heere,  […]

definitions.definition: (transitive) To assign a task to, or impose a task on.

quote.citation: 1610–1611 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tempest”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene ii]:
quote.text: All hail, great master! grave sir, hail! I come / To answer thy best pleasure; be't to fly, / To swim, to dive into the fire, to ride / On the curl'd clouds, to thy strong bidding task / Ariel and all his quality.

quote.citation: a. 1701 (date written), John Dryden, “The Last Parting of Hector and Andromache. From the Sixth Book of the Iliad.”, in The Miscellaneous Works of John Dryden, […], volume IV, London:  […]  J[acob] and R[ichard] Tonson, […], published 1760, →OCLC:
quote.text: There task thy maids, and exercise the loom.

quote.citation: 2021 May 19, “Network News: HS2 unearths 900 years of history in Buckinghamshire”, in RAIL, number 931, page 23:
quote.text: By 1966 the building was considered so unsafe that the Royal Engineers were tasked with demolishing it.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To oppress with severe or excessive burdens; to tax

quote.citation: 1851 November 14, Herman Melville, chapter 36, in Moby-Dick; or, The Whale, 1st American edition, New York, N.Y.: Harper & Brothers; London: Richard Bentley, →OCLC:
quote.text: He tasks me; he heaps me; I see in him outrageous strength, with an inscrutable malice sinewing it.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To charge, as with a fault.

quote.citation: c. 1619–1621, John Fletcher, “The Island Princesse”, in Comedies and Tragedies […], London:  […]  Humphrey Robinson, […], and for Humphrey Moseley […], published 1647, →OCLC, Act III, scene iii:
quote.text: Too impudent to task me with those errors.
